claim: Vertebrate neural tube formation depends on the coordinated orientation of cells in the tissue known as planar cell polarity (PCP).
source: Vertebrate neural tube formation depends on the coordinated orientation of cells in the tissue known as planar cell polarity (PCP).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about vertebrate neural tube formation and PCP.

claim: In the Xenopus neural plate, PCP is marked by the enrichment of the conserved proteins Prickle3 and Vangl2 at anterior cell boundaries.
source: In the Xenopus neural plate, PCP is marked by the enrichment of the conserved proteins Prickle3 and Vangl2 at anterior cell boundaries.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research and observations in the field.

claim: Par3 is planar polarized in the neuroepithelium.
source: Here we show that the apical determinant Par3 is also planar polarized in the neuroepithelium, suggesting a role for Par3 in PCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1 demonstrating Par3 enrichment at anteroposterior cell borders.

claim: Interference with Par3 activity inhibited asymmetric distribution of PCP junctional complexes.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, interference with Par3 activity inhibited asymmetric distribution of PCP junctional complexes and caused neural tube defects.
evidence: This is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2 demonstrating disrupted Vangl2 polarization.

claim: Interference with Par3 activity caused neural tube defects.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, interference with Par3 activity inhibited asymmetric distribution of PCP junctional complexes and caused neural tube defects.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis of embryos shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Par3 physically associated with Prickle3.
source: Importantly, Par3 physically associated with Prickle3 and promoted its apical localization, whereas overexpression of a Prickle3-binding Par3 fragment disrupted PCP in the neural plate.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3A-C and proximity biotinylation assays in Figure 3E.

claim: Par3 promoted apical localization of Prickle3.
source: Importantly, Par3 physically associated with Prickle3 and promoted its apical localization, whereas overexpression of a Prickle3-binding Par3 fragment disrupted PCP in the neural plate.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6 showing apical recruitment of Pk3 by Par3.

claim: Overexpression of a Prickle3-binding Par3 fragment disrupted PCP in the neural plate.
source: Importantly, Par3 physically associated with Prickle3 and promoted its apical localization, whereas overexpression of a Prickle3-binding Par3 fragment disrupted PCP in the neural plate.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing that Par3[272-544] interfered with Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization.

claim: Par3 functions by enhancing the formation of the anterior apical PCP complex.
source: We also adapted proximity biotinylation assay for use in Xenopus embryos and show that Par3 functions by enhancing the formation of the anterior apical PCP complex.
evidence: This is supported by proximity biotinylation experiments in Figure 7A-B showing reduced Vangl2 biotinylation by BL-Pk3 when Par3 is depleted or inhibited.

claim: Proximity biotinylation assay was adapted for use in Xenopus embryos.
source: We also adapted proximity biotinylation assay for use in Xenopus embryos and show that Par3 functions by enhancing the formation of the anterior apical PCP complex.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental data shown in Figures 3D-E and 7.

claim: Par3 is enriched at anteroposterior cell borders in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Par3 is enriched at AP, horizontal, cell borders (arrows) as compared to ML, vertical, cell borders.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1B with quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: ZO1 is equally distributed to all junctions in the neural plate.
source: ZO1 is equally distributed to all junctions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Par3 antibody specificity was confirmed by lack of staining in cells depleted of Par3.
source: Par3 antibody specificity was confirmed by lack of staining in the cells depleted of Par3 (Figure 1G–G').
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1G-G' showing loss of Par3 staining after morpholino injection.

claim: Unilateral injection of Par3 morpholinos inhibited neural tube closure in the majority of embryos.
source: Unilateral injection of these MOs but not the control MO into the prospective neuroectoderm inhibited neural tube closure in the majority of embryos (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C), consistent with the known roles of PCP proteins in neural tube morphogenesis (Wallingford et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The neural tube defect caused by Par3 depletion was rescued by Myc-Par3 RNA.
source: Importantly, this defect was rescued by Myc-Par3 RNA indicating specificity (Figure 2C–C').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C' demonstrating rescue of the phenotype.

claim: Vangl2 polarization at the anterior apical cell borders was disrupted in Par3-deficient neural plate cells.
source: Vangl2 polarization at the anterior apical cell borders was disrupted in Par3-deficient neural plate cells, but not in wild-type cells or those injected with control MO (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 2D-F with quantification in Figure 2E.

claim: Vangl2 is enriched basolaterally rather than apically after Par3 depletion.
source: Cryosections revealed that Vangl2 is enriched basolaterally rather than apically after Par3 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with quantification.

claim: The total amount of Vangl2 protein was not altered by Par3 depletion.
source: The total amount of Vangl2 protein was not altered (Figure 2G), indicating effect on anterior cortical localization rather than protein stability.
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot analysis in Figure 2G.

claim: Ectoderm-targeted MO injections did not significantly affect apicobasal polarity and junctional markers, including aPKC, ZO1, and β-catenin.
source: Notably, in these experiments, ectoderm-targeted MO injections did not significantly affect apicobasal polarity and junctional markers, including aPKC, ZO1, and β-catenin (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Planar polarization of Par3 was reduced in cells depleted of Vangl2.
source: We also found that planar polarization of Par3 was reduced in the cells depleted of Vangl2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that Par3 and Vangl2 reinforce each other localization in the neuroepithelium.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 with quantification.

claim: Par3 and Vangl2 reinforce each other's localization in the neuroepithelium.
source: We also found that planar polarization of Par3 was reduced in the cells depleted of Vangl2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that Par3 and Vangl2 reinforce each other localization in the neuroepithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual dependence of Par3 and Vangl2 localization shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Par3 formed a complex with Pk3 in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: We found that Par3 formed a complex with Pk3 (Figure 3A), a core PCP protein that is expressed in the superficial ectoderm (Chu et al., 2016; Ossipova et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3A.

claim: Stronger interaction was observed between Par3 and Pk3ΔPET compared to wild-type Pk3.
source: Even stronger interaction was observed with Pk3ΔPET, a deletion mutant of Pk3 that lacks a conserved PET (Prickle, Espinas and Testin) domain (Figure 3B,C), consistent with a proposed role of the PET domain in intramolecular interactions that keep Prickle in an inactive conformation (Sweede et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3B-C and is consistent with published literature.

claim: The PET domain has a proposed role in intramolecular interactions that keep Prickle in an inactive conformation.
source: Even stronger interaction was observed with Pk3ΔPET, a deletion mutant of Pk3 that lacks a conserved PET (Prickle, Espinas and Testin) domain (Figure 3B,C), consistent with a proposed role of the PET domain in intramolecular interactions that keep Prickle in an inactive conformation (Sweede et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Sweede et al., 2008.

claim: Exogenous Par3 is biotinylated by BL-Pk3 but not BL-Vangl2 in Xenopus embryos.
source: Exogenous (left) and endogenous (right) Par3 is biotinylated by BL-Pk3 but not BL-Vangl2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E by proximity biotinylation assay.

claim: Endogenous Par3 is biotinylated by BL-Pk3 but not BL-Vangl2 in Xenopus embryos.
source: Exogenous (left) and endogenous (right) Par3 is biotinylated by BL-Pk3 but not BL-Vangl2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E by proximity biotinylation assay.

claim: Par3 binds Vangl2 only in the presence of Pk3 or Pk3∆PET in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Whereas Par3, on its own, did not bind Vangl2 in transfected HEK293T cells, we found that Vangl2 was efficiently pulled down with Par3 when Pk3 or Pk3∆PET were co-expressed (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential pulldown experiments in Figure 4A.

claim: Vangl2 was not detected in pulldowns with Par3∆∆, a Par3 deletion mutant that does not bind Pk3.
source: Notably, Vangl2 was not detected in pulldowns with Par3∆∆, a Par3 deletion mutant that does not bind Pk3 (see below), indicating that Pk3 binding is necessary for the Par3-Vangl2 interaction (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A by pulldown experiments.

claim: Pk3 binding is necessary for the Par3-Vangl2 interaction.
source: Notably, Vangl2 was not detected in pulldowns with Par3∆∆, a Par3 deletion mutant that does not bind Pk3 (see below), indicating that Pk3 binding is necessary for the Par3-Vangl2 interaction (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement of Pk3 for Par3-Vangl2 interaction shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Par3, Prickle3 and Vangl2 form a ternary complex.
source: The simplest interpretation of this result is the formation of the ternary complex of Par3, Prickle3 and Vangl2.
evidence: This is inferred from the pulldown experiments in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpressed Par3 enhanced the association of Pk3 and Vangl2 within the ternary complex.
source: Notably, overexpressed Par3 enhanced the association of Pk3 and Vangl2 within the ternary complex.
evidence: This is observed in the pulldown experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The C-terminus of Par3 is sufficient for Pk3 binding.
source: The C-terminus of Par3 and the fragment including the first two PDZ domains were sufficient for Pk3 binding, whereas the N-terminus, the PDZ3 domain and the aPKC-binding site did not show any binding (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain mapping experiments in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The fragment including the first two PDZ domains of Par3 is sufficient for Pk3 binding.
source: The C-terminus of Par3 and the fragment including the first two PDZ domains were sufficient for Pk3 binding, whereas the N-terminus, the PDZ3 domain and the aPKC-binding site did not show any binding (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain mapping experiments in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The N-terminus of Par3 does not bind Pk3.
source: The C-terminus of Par3 and the fragment including the first two PDZ domains were sufficient for Pk3 binding, whereas the N-terminus, the PDZ3 domain and the aPKC-binding site did not show any binding (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain mapping experiments in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The PDZ3 domain of Par3 does not bind Pk3.
source: The C-terminus of Par3 and the fragment including the first two PDZ domains were sufficient for Pk3 binding, whereas the N-terminus, the PDZ3 domain and the aPKC-binding site did not show any binding (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain mapping experiments in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The aPKC-binding site of Par3 does not bind Pk3.
source: The C-terminus of Par3 and the fragment including the first two PDZ domains were sufficient for Pk3 binding, whereas the N-terminus, the PDZ3 domain and the aPKC-binding site did not show any binding (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain mapping experiments in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The double deletion mutant Par3∆∆ lacking PDZ1/2 and the C-terminal domain did not bind Pk3 and Pk3ΔPET.
source: However, the double deletion mutant lacking PDZ1/2 and the C-terminal domain (Par3∆∆) did not bind Pk3 and Pk3ΔPET (Figure 4D), demonstrating that these two regions of Par3 are involved in Pk3 association.
evidence: This is shown by pulldown experiments in Figure 4D.

claim: PDZ1/2 and the C-terminal domain of Par3 are involved in Pk3 association.
source: However, the double deletion mutant lacking PDZ1/2 and the C-terminal domain (Par3∆∆) did not bind Pk3 and Pk3ΔPET (Figure 4D), demonstrating that these two regions of Par3 are involved in Pk3 association.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the loss of binding in Par3∆∆ mutant shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Wild type Par3, but not Par3∆∆, was biotinylated by BL-Pk3 in Xenopus embryos.
source: Moreover, we found that wild type Par3, but not Par3∆∆, was biotinylated by BL-Pk3 in Xenopus embryos (Figure 4E), confirming the importance of the identified Pk3-binding domains for this interaction in vivo.
evidence: This is shown by proximity biotinylation assay in Figure 4E.

claim: Expression of Par3[272-544] inhibited the interaction of Par3 and Pk3 in Xenopus embryos.
source: We found that expression of Par3[272-544] but not Par3[545-756] construct in Xenopus embryos inhibited the interaction of Par3 and Pk3 as assessed by proximity biotinylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by proximity biotinylation assay in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Par3[272-544] did not affect Par3 apical localization.
source: Of note, Par3[272-544] did not affect Par3 apical localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Par3[272-544], but not Par3[545-756], interfered with Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization at the anterior cell borders.
source: We observed that Par3[272-544], but not the control fragment Par3[545-756], interfered with Pk3/Vangl2 complex polarization at the anterior cell borders (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of GFP-Pk3 localization in Figure 5A-E.

claim: The interaction of Par3 and Pk3 is essential for the formation of the functional Pk3/Vangl2 complex in neuroepithelial cells.
source: These results are consistent with our hypothesis that the interaction of Par3 and Pk3 is essential for the formation of the functional Pk3/Vangl2 complex in neuroepithelial cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the dominant-negative effect of Par3[272-544] shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both endogenous and exogenous Par3 localized to the apical side of superficial ectoderm cells.
source: Both endogenous and exogenous Par3 localized to the apical side of superficial ectoderm cells (Figure 6A–C'), consistent with other reports (Afonso and Henrique, 2006; Grego-Bessa et al., 2016; Krahn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 6A-C' and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Pk3 by itself was largely cytoplasmic in superficial ectoderm cells.
source: Whereas Pk3 by itself was largely cytoplasmic, it was recruited to the apical cortex by Par3 (Figure 6D–E'' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 6D.

claim: Pk3 was recruited to the apical cortex by Par3.
source: Whereas Pk3 by itself was largely cytoplasmic, it was recruited to the apical cortex by Par3 (Figure 6D–E'' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 6E-E'' and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The punctate cytoplasmic distribution of GFP-Dvl2 did not change in the presence of Par3.
source: By contrast, the punctate cytoplasmic distribution of GFP-Dvl2 did not change in the presence of Par3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F demonstrating specificity of Par3 effect on Pk3.

claim: Pk3 localization was not altered by the cortically localized Myc-Par1/MARK.
source: Also, Pk3 localization was not altered by the cortically localized Myc-Par1/MARK (Ossipova et al., 2007) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G,H), further confirming specificity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G,H demonstrating specificity of Par3 effect on Pk3.

claim: Vangl2 was efficiently biotinylated by BL-Pk3 in Xenopus embryos.
source: We observed that Vangl2 was efficiently biotinylated by BL-Pk3 (Figure 7A,B), consistent with the previously reported interactions of Vang and Prickle and the colocalization of Vangl2 and Pk3 in the Xenopus neural plate and the epidermis (Bastock et al., 2003; Chu et al., 2016; Chu and Sokol, 2016; Jenny et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown by proximity biotinylation assay in Figure 7A,B and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Par3N strongly reduced the Vangl2 biotinylation by BL-Pk3 in pulldown experiments.
source: Par3N strongly reduced the Vangl2 biotinylation in pulldown experiments (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by proximity biotinylation assay in Figure 7A.

claim: Vangl2 was less biotinylated in embryos depleted of Par3.
source: Similarly, Vangl2 was less biotinylated in embryos depleted of Par3 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown by proximity biotinylation assay in Figure 7B.

claim: Exogenous Pk3 and Vangl2 proteins formed anterior cortical patches in the neural plate.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Chu and Sokol, 2016; Ossipova et al., 2015c), exogenous Pk3 and Vangl2 proteins formed anterior cortical patches in the neural plate (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C,D and is consistent with previous publications.

claim: After coinjection of Par3N RNA, Pk3/Vangl2 patches were randomly distributed around the cell cortex and lacked the anterior bias.
source: By contrast, after coinjection of Par3N RNA, these patches were randomly distributed around the cell cortex and lacked the anterior bias (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is shown by analysis of GFP-Pk3 localization in Figure 7E,F.

claim: Pk3/Vangl2 complexes were not polarized in cells depleted of Par3.
source: Similarly, Pk3/Vangl2 complexes were not polarized in cells depleted of Par3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Unilateral injection of Par3N inhibited neural tube closure.
source: Moreover, unilateral injection of Par3N inhibited neural tube closure (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: This is shown by phenotypic analysis in Figure 7G-I.

claim: Par3 is required for the formation of the polarized Pk3/Vangl2 complex in the neural plate.
source: Overall, these data suggest that Par3 is required for the formation of the polarized Pk3/Vangl2 complex in the neural plate.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of Par3 depletion and dominant-negative experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Par3 polarizes in the plane of the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that Par3 polarizes in the plane of the Xenopus neural plate and is required for PCP and neural tube closure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 1.

claim: Par3 is required for PCP in the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that Par3 polarizes in the plane of the Xenopus neural plate and is required for PCP and neural tube closure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss-of-function experiments in Figures 2, 5, and 7.

claim: Par3 is required for neural tube closure in Xenopus.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that Par3 polarizes in the plane of the Xenopus neural plate and is required for PCP and neural tube closure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological analysis in Figure 2 and Figure 7.

claim: Par3 is enriched at anteroposterior cell boundaries that are parallel to the mediolateral axis of the Xenopus neural plate.
source: Par3 is enriched at anteroposterior cell boundaries that are parallel to the mediolateral axis of the Xenopus neural plate, providing evidence for the polarization of a vertebrate apicobasal polarity protein in the plane of the tissue.
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 1.

claim: The association of core PCP protein complexes with Par3 may directly contribute to Par3 enrichment at specific locations.
source: One possibility is that the association of core PCP protein complexes with Par3 may directly contribute to Par3 enrichment at specific locations (Banerjee et al., 2017; Besson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative possibility based on cited literature.

claim: In Drosophila germband, Bazooka/Par3 is enriched at dorsoventral but not anteroposterior boundaries of intercalating cells during germ-band extension along the anteroposterior axis.
source: In contrast to Xenopus Par3, fly Bazooka/Par3 is enriched at dorsoventral but not anteroposterior boundaries of intercalating cells during germ-band extension along the anteroposterior axis (Simões et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Simões et al., 2010.

claim: In the Drosophila germband, Bazooka polarity depends on Rho-associated kinase that shows complementary localization at anteroposterior cell borders.
source: Notably, in the germband, Bazooka polarity depends on Rho-associated kinase that shows complementary localization at anteroposterior cell borders (Simões et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Simões et al., 2010.

claim: In the Drosophila germband, Bazooka localization requires the LIM-domain protein Smallish.
source: In the same tissue, Bazooka localization also requires the LIM-domain protein Smallish (Beati et al., 2018), but does not seem to depend on core PCP proteins (Simões et al., 2010; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Beati et al., 2018.

claim: In the Drosophila germband, Bazooka localization does not seem to depend on core PCP proteins.
source: In the same tissue, Bazooka localization also requires the LIM-domain protein Smallish (Beati et al., 2018), but does not seem to depend on core PCP proteins (Simões et al., 2010; Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Simões et al., 2010 and Zallen and Wieschaus, 2004.

claim: In the fly eye epithelium, Bazooka is planar polarized under the control of the core PCP protein Stan/Flamingo.
source: Nevertheless, in the fly eye epithelium Bazooka is planar polarized under the control of the core PCP protein Stan/Flamingo (Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016.

claim: Tissue-specific mechanisms control Par3 planar polarization.
source: These studies indicate that tissue-specific mechanisms control Par3 planar polarization.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different tissues and organisms discussed in the text.

claim: The distribution of Par3 in the neural plate is similar to the localization of other vertebrate PCP-related complexes.
source: The distribution of Par3 in the neural plate is similar to the localization of other vertebrate PCP-related complexes (Ciruna et al., 2006; Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; McGreevy et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2012; Ossipova et al., 2015c; Shindo and Wallingford, 2014), suggesting a new role for Par3 in PCP.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature.

claim: Despite the clear morphological and molecular manifestation of Par3 depletion at neurula stages, no significant changes in the apicobasal polarity markers aPKC, ZO1, and β-catenin were detected.
source: Importantly, despite the clear morphological and molecular manifestation of Par3 depletion at neurula stages, we detected no significant changes in the apicobasal polarity markers aPKC, ZO1, and β-catenin.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No apicobasal polarity defects have been reported for par3 mutant follicular epithelial cells in Drosophila.
source: Similarly, no apicobasal polarity defects have been reported for par3 mutant follicular epithelial cells in Drosophila (Shahab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Shahab et al., 2015.

claim: Apicobasal polarity markers did not change in retinal endothelial cells of par3 knockout mice.
source: Also, apicobasal polarity markers did not change in retinal endothelial cells of par3 knockout mice (Hikita et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Hikita et al., 2018.

claim: The requirement of Par3 for apicobasal polarity may depend on developmental context and cell type.
source: Thus, the requirement of Par3 for apicobasal polarity may depend on developmental context and cell type.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of different experimental systems.

claim: The novel function of Par3 in the neural plate PCP is consistent with the requirement of Par3 in zebrafish neural tube morphogenesis.
source: The novel function of Par3 in the neural plate PCP is consistent with the requirement of Par3 in zebrafish neural tube morphogenesis (Tawk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Tawk et al., 2007.

claim: A recent study has implicated rare Par3 variants in human cranial neural tube defects.
source: Supporting our hypothesis, a recent study has implicated rare Par3 variants in human cranial neural tube defects (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Par3 -/- mouse embryos lack neural tube abnormalities.
source: This contrasts lack of neural tube abnormalities in Par3 -/- mouse embryos (Hirose et al., 2006) that could be due to functional redundancy (Ishiuchi and Takeichi, 2011; Kohjima et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Hirose et al., 2006.

claim: The lack of neural tube abnormalities in Par3 -/- mouse embryos could be due to functional redundancy.
source: This contrasts lack of neural tube abnormalities in Par3 -/- mouse embryos (Hirose et al., 2006) that could be due to functional redundancy (Ishiuchi and Takeichi, 2011; Kohjima et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on cited literature.

claim: Proximity biotinylation detects both stable and transient protein-protein interactions.
source: This technique detects both stable and transient protein-protein interactions (Roux et al., 2018), and will help dissect cell signaling events leading to PCP.
evidence: This is cited from Roux et al., 2018.

claim: The Par3/Pk3 interaction is critical for neuroepithelial polarization.
source: Consistent with the critical role of the Par3/Pk3 interaction, we show that the Pk3-binding fragment Par3[272-544] specifically inhibits asymmetric distribution of PCP complexes in the neuroepithelial cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dominant-negative effect shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Par3 construct that does not bind Pk3 failed to interfere with body axis elongation.
source: Moreover, the Par3 construct that does not bind Pk3 failed to interfere with body axis elongation that is commonly associated with PCP signaling (Gray et al., 2011; Sokol, 2000; Wallingford et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ability of Par3 to bind Pk3 and recruit it to the apical membrane may be a prerequisite for the formation of functional PCP complexes at the apical anterior cell borders.
source: The ability of Par3 to bind Pk3 and recruit it to the apical membrane may be a prerequisite for the formation of functional PCP complexes at the apical anterior cell borders (Figure 7J)(Ossipova et al., 2015a; Ossipova et al., 2015c).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results and is illustrated in the working model in Figure 7J.

claim: Both the dominant interfering Par3N construct and Par3 depletion reduced the biotinylation of Vangl2 by BL-Pk3.
source: Moreover, both the dominant interfering Par3N construct and Par3 depletion reduced the biotinylation of Vangl2 by BL-Pk3, supporting the view that Par3-dependent apical recruitment of Pk3 is essential for PCP complex formation.
evidence: This is shown by proximity biotinylation assays in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Par3-dependent apical recruitment of Pk3 is essential for PCP complex formation.
source: Moreover, both the dominant interfering Par3N construct and Par3 depletion reduced the biotinylation of Vangl2 by BL-Pk3, supporting the view that Par3-dependent apical recruitment of Pk3 is essential for PCP complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the proximity biotinylation results in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Par3 may recruit Pk3 to the apical domain by altering apical membrane properties.
source: Whereas the direct binding of Pk3 by Par3 is the simplest interpretation of our data, alternatively, Par3 may recruit Pk3 to the apical domain by altering apical membrane properties (Ahmed and Macara, 2017; Bryant et al., 2010; Ruch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: It is currently unknown whether the Par3/Pk3 interaction is modulated by other Par3-associated proteins, such as Par6, JAM-A or Nectin.
source: It is currently unknown whether the Par3/Pk3 interaction is modulated by other Par3-associated proteins, such as Par6, JAM-A or Nectin (Ebnet et al., 2001; Joberty et al., 2000; Takekuni et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge with references to Par3-associated proteins.

claim: The interaction of Par3 with the core PCP machinery is required for the formation of apical PCP complexes.
source: Taken together, our experiments indicate that the interaction of Par3 with the core PCP machinery is required for the formation of apical PCP complexes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: In Drosophila blastoderm, Par3 stimulates E-cadherin recruitment to apicolateral junctions.
source: These findings parallel studies in Drosophila blastoderm where Par3 stimulates E-cadherin recruitment to apicolateral junctions (McGill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from McGill et al., 2009.

claim: Par3 promotes intestinal epithelial cell polarization by interacting with E-cadherin and other polarity proteins in C. elegans embryos.
source: Par3 also promotes intestinal epithelial cell polarization by interacting with E-cadherin and other polarity proteins in C. elegans embryos (Achilleos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Achilleos et al., 2010.

claim: Apical enrichment of PCP complexes may be directly responsible for neural plate PCP.
source: Apical enrichment of PCP complexes that we observe may be directly responsible for neural plate PCP or can modulate other cellular processes that ultimately contribute to neural tube closure, such as radial and mediolateral cell intercalation, apical constriction or centrosome and cilia functions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed apical enrichment.

claim: Apical enrichment of PCP complexes can modulate other cellular processes that ultimately contribute to neural tube closure, such as radial and mediolateral cell intercalation, apical constriction or centrosome and cilia functions.
source: Apical enrichment of PCP complexes that we observe may be directly responsible for neural plate PCP or can modulate other cellular processes that ultimately contribute to neural tube closure, such as radial and mediolateral cell intercalation, apical constriction or centrosome and cilia functions.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation of the observed apical enrichment.

claim: Both Par3 and core PCP proteins were implicated in radial intercalation of multiciliated epidermal cells.
